# A Commonsense Investment in America's Workforce: The Case for a Federal Four-Day Work Week Tax Credit

## Executive Summary

American families are working harder than ever, and it's time our tax code rewarded the employers who are finding smarter ways to get results without burning out their people. A federal tax credit for companies that adopt a four-day work week is a pragmatic, evidence-backed investment in the middle class — not a mandate, but an incentive that lets the market lead. The largest real-world test of this idea, the UK's six-month pilot with 61 companies, found that revenue stayed flat to slightly positive (up 1.4% on average) while sick days fell 65% and 71% of employees reported less burnout [1][2]. Ninety-two percent of participating firms kept the policy after the trial ended [2]. We already have bipartisan precedent for using targeted tax credits — like the Work Opportunity Tax Credit and SECURE Act 2.0 startup credits — to nudge employer behavior toward better outcomes for workers [3][4]. This proposal follows that same tested playbook: give businesses a reason to modernize, let the data guide adoption, and deliver working families more time with less risk to the bottom line.

problem.section_markdown:
## The Problem

American families are working harder and getting squeezed harder — and Washington has offered little beyond platitudes. Burnout isn't a fringe complaint; it's the default condition of the modern workplace. A 2023 Gallup survey found that 76% of employees experience burnout at least sometimes, with 28% reporting they feel burned out "very often" or "always" at work [1]. That's not a productivity story, it's a public-health and family-stability story: exhausted parents miss soccer games, exhausted workers make more errors, and exhausted employees quit — costing employers the very talent they spent years training.

This is a solvable problem, and the data on solutions is unusually strong for something so new. When 61 UK companies piloted a four-day, 32-hour week at full pay under the rigorous "100-80-100" model — 100% pay, 80% time, 100% output — the results, tracked by researchers at Cambridge, Boston College, and the think tank Autonomy, were striking: sick days fell by 65%, revenue held roughly steady, and 71% of employees reported reduced burnout [2]. Ninety-two percent of participating firms chose to keep the shorter week after the trial ended [2]. This isn't a European curiosity or a lifestyle indulgence for a lucky few — it's an evidence-based operational model that boosted retention and time-to-fill on job postings by roughly a third in follow-on analysis [3].

The real problem, then, isn't whether reduced-hour scheduling works — the pilots answer that. It's that no market mechanism currently helps small and mid-sized employers absorb the transition costs of redesigning workflows, especially in sectors without the cash cushion of a tech firm running its own experiment. That's a gap smart, targeted federal policy can close.

4 Day Week Global / Medium, UK 2023 Results

solution.section_markdown:
## The Solution & Why It Aligns With Our Values

The proposal is straightforward: a federal tax credit for employers who transition employees to a four-day, forty-hour-or-reduced-hour work week without cutting pay. Rather than mandating a one-size-fits-all schedule from Washington, the credit works the way good policy should — it uses the tax code to nudge private employers toward a practice many are already testing voluntarily, while letting each business tailor implementation to its own industry and workforce. That is public-private partnership in its most practical form: government lowers the cost of experimentation, and employers supply the operational know-how to make it work.

This fits comfortably within a pragmatic, evidence-based governing philosophy because it does not ask anyone to take reduced-hours scheduling on faith. Companies and public agencies in the U.S., U.K., and elsewhere have piloted compressed schedules over the past several years, and firms have generally reported it as workable enough to continue after the trial period — a track record of voluntary adoption that is itself meaningful evidence, even where rigorous, peer-reviewed productivity numbers are still being established. A modest, opt-in tax credit lets more employers generate their own real-world data before anyone commits to permanent change — exactly the kind of incremental, test-and-scale approach that has guided successful federal initiatives from R&D credits to renewable energy incentives.

It is also squarely a middle-class opportunity policy. Workers get more time for caregiving, further education, or a second income stream, without sacrificing take-home pay — the kind of tangible, kitchen-table benefit that resonates far more than abstract economic indicators. And because the credit rewards employers rather than penalizing those who don't participate, it avoids the government-overreach objections that sink more heavy-handed labor mandates, instead building a coalition of business leaders who see workforce flexibility as a competitive advantage in attracting talent. That is inclusive growth: expanding what work can look like for working families while keeping the system employers and workers already know intact.

recommendations.section_markdown:
## Recommendations

A policy this pragmatic doesn't need to be complicated — it needs champions who can move it through committee, sell it at the doorstep, and get it into a bipartisan vehicle. Here's the game plan:

1. **Draft a narrowly scoped tax credit pilot.** Model it on the UK trial design that produced [1] a 57% drop in staff turnover and a 35% revenue increase for participating firms [2] — start with a 3-5 year sunset and mandatory third-party evaluation so we can prove out the ROI before scaling.
2. **Recruit co-sponsors across the aisle.** Frame it to moderate Republicans as a business-productivity and small-government incentive (a credit, not a mandate) rather than a labor mandate — this is how bipartisan tax credits like the R&D credit and Work Opportunity Tax Credit have survived multiple Congresses.
3. **Attach it to a must-pass tax extenders package** rather than a standalone bill, where targeted employer credits have historically had their best shot at floor time.
4. **Prioritize outreach to mid-size employers and the care, tech, and professional-services sectors**, where UK pilot firms reported the strongest productivity gains [1], to build a coalition of real-world business success stories for hearings.
5. **Pair legislative asks with local advocacy**: state chambers of commerce, small-business associations, and worker-advocacy groups should submit joint letters of support to Ways and Means and Finance Committee members.
6. **Commission a nonpartisan CBO/JCT score early** to preempt cost objections and demonstrate fiscal responsibility.
7. **Build the narrative around family stability and retention savings**, not ideology — evidence-based, kitchen-table, and built to last past a single administration.

# A Federal Tax Credit for the Four-Day Work Week: Time Is a Justice Issue

## Executive Summary

Working people built this country's wealth, and it's time we got our time back. A federal tax credit for employers who adopt a four-day work week is a concrete, winnable step toward an economy that serves the many, not corporate boards and shareholders. The world's largest four-day week pilot, run in the UK, found that 92% of participating companies kept the shorter week after the trial ended, with 18 making it permanent [1]. Workers in these trials reported dramatically reduced burnout and better mental and physical health, while productivity held steady or improved [2]. This isn't charity for bosses — it's a public incentive that rewards employers who share productivity gains with workers instead of hoarding them, while giving working families more time for caregiving, organizing, rest, and community life. Paired with strong labor standards so the credit can't be used to cut pay or intensify workloads, this policy is a down payment on the four-day week as a right for all workers, not a perk for the privileged few.

problem.section_markdown:
## The Problem

Working people in this country are being worked to the bone while the wealth we create keeps flowing upward. For decades, corporate America has demanded more hours, more output, and more "flexibility" from workers — while giving back stagnant wages, disappearing pensions, and relentless burnout. The standard five-day, forty-hour week was designed for a different economy, one where a single paycheck could support a family and where productivity gains were shared between workers and owners. That deal has been broken. Today, productivity has climbed for generations while the benefits have been captured almost entirely by executives and shareholders, not the workers who actually generate the value. Meanwhile, working families are stretched thinner than ever — juggling caregiving, second jobs, long commutes, and chronic exhaustion, with Black, Brown, and low-wage workers bearing the heaviest toll from schedules designed around corporate convenience rather than human need. Burnout, stress-related illness, and time poverty are not personal failings; they are the predictable result of an economic system that treats our time as an infinite resource to be extracted rather than a finite gift to be respected. Employers who might voluntarily experiment with shorter, more humane schedules face real short-term cost and competitive pressure to conform to the exploitative status quo, so without public policy tipping the scales, corporate power will keep defaulting to overwork. This is a structural problem, not an individual one — and it demands a structural, federal response that rewards employers for choosing workers' well-being over extraction, and begins to rebalance power between labor and capital.

solution.section_markdown:
## The Solution & Why It Aligns With Our Values

The fix is straightforward: a federal tax credit that rewards employers for cutting the workweek to four days at no loss in pay. Companies that make the shift — protecting workers' wages while giving them back a full day of their lives — get a direct offset against their tax bill. It's a public incentive that pushes the private sector toward a fairer bargain, rather than leaving working people to beg bosses for scraps of their own time.

This is worker power written into the tax code. For generations, gains in productivity and automation have flowed almost entirely to executives, shareholders, and the billionaire class, while the people actually doing the work have been squeezed for more hours and less security. A four-day week, subsidized by public dollars but earned through workers' labor and organizing, is a way of clawing back a piece of that stolen time. It says explicitly: the fruits of a more productive economy belong to the many who create that productivity, not just the few who own the means of production.

It also advances racial and economic justice. Low-wage and shift workers — disproportionately Black, Brown, and immigrant workers — face the worst scheduling instability and the least control over their own time. A federal push toward shorter, stable, well-paid schedules starts to chip away at that exploitation industry by industry.

This policy is a natural fit for our movement because it treats time, like housing and healthcare, as a matter of dignity, not a privilege reserved for the already-comfortable. It uses the tax code — a tool the wealthy have long bent to serve concentrated capital — to instead serve the collective good, rewarding companies that choose people over pure profit extraction. Paired with strong union organizing and enforcement so employers can't game the credit or quietly cut pay, this is one more concrete step toward an economy and a democracy built for working people, not corporate boardrooms.

recommendations.section_markdown:
## Recommendations

The path to the tax credit runs through building on momentum already in motion — Sen. Bernie Sanders' Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act shows there's real appetite in Congress for shortening the workweek without cutting pay [1] — and turning worksite proof points, like the UK's 61-company pilot where 92% of employers kept the four-day model after seeing performance hold steady [2], into political leverage. Here's how we move it:

1. **Pair the credit with a no-pay-cut mandate.** Push staffers to condition eligibility on maintaining full wages and benefits, so employers can't pocket the credit while quietly cutting workers' take-home pay.
2. **Build a floor, not a loophole.** Insist any credit exclude employers who've committed union-busting violations or wage theft — the money should reward good actors, not subsidize exploitation.
3. **Center union locals in coalition-building.** Organize labor councils, especially in service and care industries, to testify and lobby, using existing legislative allies like Rep. Mark Takano [3] as anchors.
4. **Demand racial and gender equity data.** Require reporting on which workers (by race, gender, industry) actually get the four-day benefit, preventing it from becoming a white-collar-only perk.
5. **Mobilize base testimonials.** Collect worker stories from four-day pilots to counter corporate lobbying that claims productivity losses.
6. **Sunset and study.** Advocate for a built-in review after three years to expand the credit or convert it into a binding standard, following the arc of the Sanders bill toward a full 32-hour week [1].

Every step should keep the fight framed as workers reclaiming time and power from corporate control — not a favor granted by employers.

problem.section_markdown:
## The Problem

Folks, the American worker has been getting squeezed for decades — and Washington's response has always been more regulations, more mandates, and more lectures from people who've never punched a clock in their life. Meanwhile, roughly half of U.S. workers report experiencing burnout right now, driven by heavy workloads, financial stress, and being tethered to the job 24/7 through phones and email [1]. That's not a "woke workplace culture" problem — that's a real problem hitting truckers, machinists, nurses, and small-business employees in every red county in this country.

Here's the kicker: the same D.C. establishment that lectures Americans about "work-life balance" has done nothing to actually help working families reclaim their time. Big corporations and Silicon Valley elites experiment with perks for their own white-collar staff while the guy running the shop floor in Ohio or the diner in rural Pennsylvania gets none of it. The overseas trials prove the concept works when businesses are actually incentivized to try it — in the UK's landmark four-day week trial, sick-day absences dropped 65% and staff turnover fell, all while businesses kept revenue steady [2]. More than 90% of the companies that ran the experiment kept the shorter week afterward because it worked for their bottom line and their people [2].

The real problem isn't that American businesses can't compete with a leaner, smarter schedule — it's that nobody in Washington has given them a reason to try. Small manufacturers and family businesses operate on thin margins and can't just gamble on restructuring their workweek without support. That's a policy failure, not a worker failure — and it's exactly the kind of common-sense gap this proposal is built to close.

solution.section_markdown:
## The Solution & Why It Aligns With Our Values

Here's the fix: a federal tax credit for any American employer — small business, factory, family farm operation — that shifts its workforce to a four-day week without cutting pay. Simple, voluntary, no mandate from Washington telling a business owner how to run his shop. That's the whole point. This isn't some European-style bureaucratic decree; it's a carrot, not a stick, and it goes straight to the job creators who actually build things in this country instead of the consultants and paper-pushers in D.C. who've never met a payroll they had to make.

Why does it fit our values? Because this is about giving power back to the American worker and the American employer, not to some unelected agency. For decades the working man in this country has been squeezed — commuting hours he'll never get back, missing his kid's ballgame, burning out while multinational corporations and government bureaucracies shuffle him around like a number. A four-day week, backed by a tax incentive instead of a regulation, says: we trust business owners to figure out what works for their own operation, and we're going to reward the ones bold enough to put their employees — and their families — first.

This is also a jobs and manufacturing play. A tax credit rewards firms that keep production domestic and keep workers on the books full-time with full pay, rather than off-shoring or automating them away. It strengthens the American family by giving Mom and Dad an extra day home — for church, for the kids, for the things that actually matter — without Big Government forcing a one-size-fits-all rule on every business in the country.

And because it's structured as a tax credit, not a mandate, it respects federalism and free enterprise: no business is forced to comply, no bureaucrat gets to police your break room. It's targeted relief for employers willing to try something bold for their people — exactly the kind of common-sense, worker-first, government-out-of-the-way policy that puts America and forgotten families first.

recommendations.section_markdown:
## Recommendations

Folks, drain-the-swamp talk is cheap — here's the actual game plan to get this done for working families instead of letting it die in some subcommittee run by lobbyists and lifers. This is an America First, pro-business, pro-worker win, and here's how we push it across the finish line:

1. **Draft it as a targeted tax credit, not a mandate.** Model language on state-level efforts like the Massachusetts bill that rewards employers who move at least 15 workers to a four-day week without cutting pay [1] — keep it voluntary so Washington isn't dictating to Main Street business owners.

2. **Kill the union-boss overtime traps.** Make sure our version avoids the daily-overtime landmines buried in the Sanders-style 32-hour mandate bill [2], which just pads paperwork and punishes small manufacturers. We want incentives, not another regulatory hammer from the Biden-Sanders wing.

3. **Recruit red-state small business coalitions** to testify that this credit means real relief, not more D.C. red tape — small business owners already back similar credit-based tax relief by wide margins [1].

4. **Target rural manufacturers and family-owned shops first** in pilot outreach — they're the forgotten backbone of this country and the first ones who should see the benefit.

5. **Frame every press release around freedom and family** — parents home for their kids, churches full on Sundays, not bureaucrats deciding your schedule.

6. **Get it attached to a must-pass tax package**, not left as a standalone bill that dies quietly.

7. **Activists: flood town halls and local papers** — force your Representative to go on record for American families, not the swamp.

summary.section_markdown:
# A Market-Based Case for a Federal Four-Day Work Week Tax Credit

## Executive Summary

American employers, not Washington mandates, should decide how to structure the workweek — but the tax code can still be used wisely to reward businesses that find smarter, leaner ways to compete for talent. A targeted federal tax credit for employers voluntarily offering a four-day work week is not a labor mandate; it is a market-tested incentive that rewards efficiency, boosts small-business competitiveness against larger firms with bigger benefits budgets, and helps address chronic worker shortages without expanding the regulatory state. Structured properly — with a sunset clause, a cost cap, and eligibility limited to firms that maintain output — this credit costs taxpayers far less than permanent entitlement expansions, strengthens Main Street's ability to attract workers without raising wages through inflationary government spending, and lets the private sector, not bureaucrats, define what "flexibility" means for each industry. It is fiscally disciplined, pro-growth, federalist in spirit, and rooted in the conservative principle that voluntary market experimentation beats one-size-fits-all mandates every time.

problem.section_markdown:
## The Problem

America's small and mid-sized employers are fighting a two-front war: a labor market where skilled workers are scarce and expensive to replace, and a regulatory and tax code that rewards nobody for experimenting with better ways to retain them. Turnover, absenteeism, and burnout impose real costs on the bottom line — costs that fall hardest on the small businesses least able to absorb them, since they lack the HR departments and benefits budgets of large corporations. Employers who want to compete for talent by rethinking the workweek currently have to eat every dollar of the transition cost themselves, with no help from Washington, even though a more productive, less burned-out workforce ultimately means more taxable business income, more consumer spending, and less strain on federal safety-net programs.

Meanwhile, Washington already spends heavily — and often inefficiently — on workforce and labor policy through one-size-fits-all mandates that raise compliance costs without proof of results. That is precisely backward. The tax code should not penalize employers for innovating on scheduling any more than it should punish them for adopting new technology. Right now it does neither reward nor even acknowledge voluntary workplace innovation, leaving a policy vacuum that heavy-handed state and local mandates are increasingly rushing to fill with rigid, compliance-driven rules rather than market-tested flexibility.

The result is a missed opportunity: businesses that want to pilot a four-day week to cut overhead, reduce turnover, and sharpen recruiting have to do so with zero federal support, while competitors who stick with the status quo face no penalty for higher churn. A targeted, opt-in tax credit would let the market — not a federal mandate — sort out which employers and industries benefit, filling the gap between costly government overreach and total federal indifference to a genuinely promising business practice.

solution.section_markdown:
## The Solution & Why It Aligns With Our Values

This proposal creates a targeted, opt-in federal tax credit for employers that voluntarily transition to a four-day, 32-hour work week without cutting employee pay. Unlike a mandate, it changes no labor law, imposes no new compliance regime, and leaves every business owner free to decide whether the model fits their operation. That distinction matters: this is incentive-based policy, not command-and-control regulation, and it puts the choice where it belongs — in the hands of the employer who knows their industry, their customers, and their bottom line.

The economic case is sound. Independent trials have found that employees on a reduced 33-hour schedule sustain output comparable to a traditional 38-hour week [1], and a widely cited pilot program reported gains in worker health, lower stress, and reduced absenteeism without productivity loss [2]. For small and mid-size firms competing against larger companies for talent, a tax credit that helps offset the transition costs of restructuring scheduling, workflows, and client coverage is a smart, limited-government way to help them compete — rather than layering on a Washington mandate that a big corporation can absorb but a 20-person shop cannot.

This is precisely the kind of federalism-friendly, market-oriented tool our coalition should champion: it uses the tax code, not the regulatory code, to encourage innovation. It rewards voluntary experimentation rather than punishing noncompliance, and it respects that American small businesses already carry billions in existing federal paperwork and reporting burdens [3]. A modest, sunset-able credit — paid for and scored against real productivity data — lets the market test a scheduling innovation on its own merits, with government simply lowering the cost of trying something new. That is limited government at its best: not picking winners, but clearing a path for employers to compete, retain workers, and grow.

recommendations.section_markdown:
## Recommendations

The path forward is not a federal mandate — it's a market test, structured the way conservatives structure any tax expenditure: time-limited, capped, and rigorously measured. Here's how to move it from white paper to markup.

1. **Draft a sunset-clause bill.** Model federal legislation on the pilot-program approach states like Maryland and Pennsylvania have already introduced, which pair a capped employer tax credit with a defined trial period rather than a permanent entitlement [1].
2. **Cap the fiscal exposure up front.** Set an aggregate national credit ceiling and a per-employer cap — comparable in spirit to Maryland's proposed $750,000-per-employer, two-credit limit — so scoring stays predictable for CBO and appropriators [1].
3. **Restrict eligibility to small and mid-sized employers.** Target firms under a defined headcount to keep the benefit aimed at Main Street job creators, not subsidize Fortune 500 payroll decisions they can already afford to make unilaterally.
4. **Require independent productivity and retention reporting** as a condition of the credit, using metrics comparable to those tracked in the 4 Day Week Global US/Ireland trials — including productivity, revenue, and retention outcomes — so Congress can judge return on taxpayer investment before any extension [2].
5. **Build in an automatic sunset and reauthorization vote** after three years, forcing a genuine cost-benefit review rather than letting the credit calcify into permanent spending.
6. **Coordinate with state chambers of commerce** already tracking similar bills in Massachusetts and California to build a multi-state coalition and avoid duplicative compliance regimes [3].
7. **Engage small-business associations early** to co-author eligibility criteria, ensuring the credit reduces red tape rather than adding a new compliance burden.

Activists should press members for cosponsorship on a lean, sunsetted bill — not a broader workweek mandate — and staffers should request a CBO score before any hearing to keep the fiscal case airtight.
